advisories.title: Concurrent requests can redeem one authorization code or pushed request_uri more than once
Third-party OAuth app can steal a user's live upstream social/SSO provider access tokens via the Account API (missing assertFirstPartyClient on the third-party-token endpoints)
SAML application authentication endpoint accepts XML that is not well-formed
Email/SMS connector credentials returned in the API response body and stored in audit logs on an outbound network error
advisories.summary:
> [!NOTE]
> **Fixed in Logto 1.46.0** (https://github.com/logto-io/logto/pull/9849). Upgrade to 1.46.0 or later. The fix is in Logto core, so connectors don't need updating.

---

I am the author of logto-io/logto#9849 (sanitizing `got` errors in the core error handler). While addressing a review comment on that PR, I found a related issue that goes beyond logging, so I am reporting it privately through this advisory.

## Summary

When an outbound request made by a connector fails at the network level (timeout, connection reset, DNS failure), several connectors wrap the raw `got` `RequestError` in a `ConnectorError`:

- `packages/connectors/connector-sendgrid-email/src/index.ts` (`throw new ConnectorError(ConnectorErrorCodes.General, error)`)
- `connector-mailgun`, `connector-http-email`, `connector-smtp2go-email`, `connector-saml` do the same.

A `got` `RequestError` carries the full request `Options` as an enumerable property, and `Options.toJSON()` returns its internals: headers (including `Authorization: Bearer <SendGrid API key>`), `username`/`password` (Mailgun basic auth, also embedded in the serialized `url` as `https://api:<key>@api.mailgun.net/...`), `json`/`form` bodies (recipient address, verification code).

Two sinks then expose that object:

1. **HTTP response body.** `packages/core/src/middleware/koa-connector-error-handler.ts` converts the `ConnectorError` into `new RequestError({ code: 'connector.general', status: 400, errorDescription: JSON.stringify(data) }, data)`. `RequestError.toBody()` (`packages/core/src/errors/RequestError/index.ts`) returns `pick(this, 'code', 'data', 'details')`, so `data` - the serialized `got` error with the credentials - is sent to the caller. The `errorDescription` interpolation also puts the same JSON in the i18n `message`.
2. **Audit logs.** `packages/core/src/middleware/koa-audit-log.ts` stores `pick(error, 'message', 'code', 'data')` in the `logs` table, which is readable in the Console and through the Management API.

The endpoints that send a verification code (`POST /api/verification-codes`, the experience API `.../verifications/verification-code`, `routes-me/verification-code`) are reachable without authentication, so an anonymous caller who requests a code during a provider outage receives the provider API key in a 400 response.

## Reproduction (reasoning, verified at the unit level)

```js
import { RequestError, Options } from 'got';
import { ConnectorError, ConnectorErrorCodes } from '@logto/connector-kit';

const options = new Options('https://api.sendgrid.com/v3/mail/send', {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: { Authorization: 'Bearer SG.FAKE' },
  json: { from: 'a@b.c' },
});
const gotError = new RequestError('Timeout awaiting request', { code: 'ETIMEDOUT' }, options);
const wrapped = new ConnectorError(ConnectorErrorCodes.General, gotError);

wrapped.message.includes('SG.FAKE');                       // true
JSON.stringify({ data: wrapped.data }).includes('SG.FAKE'); // true - what toBody() returns
```

End to end: configure the SendGrid connector, make `api.sendgrid.com` unreachable (hosts file or egress rule), then `POST /api/verification-codes` with an email address. The 400 body contains `data.options.headers.authorization`.

## Suggested fix

Never let a raw `got` error become `data`. Either:

- in `@logto/connector-kit`, make `ConnectorError` reduce an `Error` passed as `data` to `{ name, code, message }` (drop `options`, `request`, `response`), which fixes every connector at once; or
- in `koa-connector-error-handler.ts`, sanitize `data` before building the `RequestError` (the `sanitizeError` helper from #9849 can be reused), and never interpolate the raw JSON into `errorDescription`;
- and in the email/SMS connectors, pass `error.message` rather than the error object (as `connector-vonage-sms` already does).

## Impact note

Self-hosted deployments that use the SendGrid, Mailgun, SMTP2GO or HTTP email connectors are affected on every network-level failure to...

advisories.title: One-time token can be verified twice concurrently due to missing status predicate in UPDATE query
advisories.summary:
## Summary

Logto's one-time token verification contains a TOCTOU race condition. The `verifyOneTimeToken()` function reads a token's status as Active, validates it, then issues an UPDATE query that has no WHERE status = Active predicate. Under PostgreSQL Read Committed isolation, two concurrent transactions can both read Active, both pass validation, and both update the row to Consumed - each returning success to the caller.

## Impact

A one-time password-reset token or magic-link token that should be single-use can be consumed by two concurrent flows:
- Password reset replay: An attacker with the token can race the verification to establish two independent password-reset sessions and call resetPassword() on each to set a password of their choice (account takeover).
- Magic-link dual sign-in: Two tabs loading the same sign-in token URL can both complete sign-in, creating two authenticated sessions from one token.

## Root Cause

packages/core/src/queries/one-time-tokens.ts has an updateOneTimeTokenStatus function that issues:
  UPDATE one_time_tokens SET status = Consumed WHERE token = $token RETURNING *
There is no AND status = Active predicate. Both concurrent writers succeed.

packages/core/src/libraries/one-time-token.ts#verifyOneTimeToken() performs a read-then-write: checkOneTimeToken() reads and validates the token is Active, then updateOneTimeTokenStatus() updates to Consumed without checking current status.

Under PostgreSQL Read Committed:
- T1 reads status=Active (passes check)
- T2 reads status=Active (passes check, T1 has not committed yet)
- T1 UPDATE to Consumed, commits
- T2 UPDATE to Consumed (finds row by token, no status predicate - succeeds)

## Affected Routes

- Management API: POST /api/one-time-tokens/verify
- Experience API: POST /experience/verification/one-time-token/verify
- Forgot-password flow: identifyForgotPasswordWithOneTimeToken()

## Proof

PostgreSQL-backed concurrency test: 30/30 race iterations both transactions successfully verified the same Active token (100% reproduction).

## Remediation

Add AND status = Active to the UPDATE WHERE clause:
  UPDATE one_time_tokens SET status = Consumed WHERE token = $token AND status = Active RETURNING *

## Credit

Anonymous researcher

advisories.title: logto vulnerable to SAML authentication bypass via unchecked assertion audience
advisories.summary:
### Summary

Logto's SAML enterprise SSO connector accepts an assertion the configured identity provider signed for a different service provider, and completes a sign-in as whichever user that assertion names. This was reproduced end to end against the current release, and every release since 1.12.0 carries the route it was reproduced through. The affected-range note sets out the one place below that the range could turn out wider, and why that is not claimed.

`handleSamlAssertion` builds a samlify `ServiceProvider` from the connector's SP entityID and the identity provider certificate, calls `parseLoginResponse`, and returns the parsed extract. samlify verifies the signature, the issuer and the `Conditions` time window, and its documentation assigns `AudienceRestriction`, the bearer `SubjectConfirmationData` `Recipient`, the response `Destination` and `InResponseTo` to the caller. Logto reads none of them, at any revision since the class was added. A signature proves which identity provider issued an assertion. The audience is the field that says which application it was issued to. With the audience unread, Logto's assertion consumer service treats every assertion that identity provider signs under the configured issuer as a valid sign-in, whatever application it was minted for, and the sign-in ends in OIDC tokens for the applications of that Logto tenant.

Two consequences were measured against the released image with a Keycloak realm as the identity provider, which signs every SAML client in the realm with one realm key under one realm issuer. A response the realm addressed to another application, posted to Logto's assertion consumer service, completed sign-in with the same `sub` and the same `email` as the baseline response addressed to Logto's own service provider. And the identity provider cannot withhold access to Logto: with Logto's own SAML client set `enabled=false` at the realm, the normal sign-in path is refused at the identity provider before any login, while that same foreign response still issues an id_token for the user. An operator who removes Logto from a user at the identity provider has not removed it.

### Affected range, and how each end was established

The lower bound is the first release carrying the enterprise SSO assertion consumer service, `/authn/${ssoPath}/saml/:connectorId`, which is the route this report reproduces. It arrives in `edb2bdcce`, "feat(core): add the saml assertion handle flow (#4872)", committed 2023-11-17T06:14:45Z: absent from `packages/core/src/routes/authn.ts` at the `v1.11.0` tag, registered at line 175 of that file at `v1.12.0`. That commit lands after the `v1.11.0` tag, dated 2023-11-14T11:57:42Z, and before the `v1.12.0` tag, dated 2023-12-06T08:13:56Z.

The upper end is measured rather than inferred. The behaviour was reproduced end to end on the official `svhd/logto:1.45.0` image, the release tagged 2026-10-13T07:30:57Z, on two independently built rigs, through that same route.

There is one place the range could turn out wider, and it is deliberately not claimed. The unchecked helper predates the route it is usually reached through: `40a5a18d9`, "feat(core): add saml sso class", authored 2023-11-02T03:17:34Z and committed 2023-11-07T04:01:35Z, and the earliest release carrying it is 1.11.0, found by enumerating the `v*` tags that contain that commit and sorting them by tag date rather than by name. At `v1.11.0` the helper sits at `packages/core/src/sso/SamlConnector/utils.ts:137` with the same `parseLoginResponse` call and no audience read: a case-insensitive search of that whole file at that tag for `audience` and `InResponseTo` returns nothing, and the only match for `destination` is a local variable in the attribute-mapping code at line 114, unrelated to a response `Destination`. An HTTP route reaches it there, and that route names SAML nowhere, dispatching on the stored connector's provider name instead: `POST /interaction/single-sign-on/:connectorId/...

advisories.title: MFA bypass: switching interaction event SignIn→Register after identification skips second-factor verification
MFA bypass: a verified enterprise-SSO or sign-in-passkey verification record not bound to the identified user skips the mandatory second factor
advisories.summary:
## Summary

Logto skips the mandatory second factor for a sign-in whenever the interaction holds a verified
**enterprise SSO** or **sign-in passkey** verification record, without checking that the record is
the one the interaction identified its account with. The same unchecked condition also exempts the
interaction from the mandatory MFA **enrollment** requirement.

An attacker who holds a first factor for the target account - a leaked or phished password, for
example - and who can place one verified enterprise SSO or sign-in passkey record in the same
interaction therefore completes the sign-in without the account holder's second factor, and a
session is issued for the target account.

## Details

All references are in `packages/core/src/routes/experience/`.

The tenant MFA policy is applied at two points in `classes/experience-interaction.ts`, and both
tested only whether such a record was present:

- `isMfaGateFulfilled()`, consulted by `guardMfaVerificationStatus()`, which decides whether a
  second factor has to be verified. It returned before the interaction's account was resolved at
  all.
- the `assertMfaFulfilled()` condition in `submit()`, which decides whether an account under a
  mandatory policy has to enroll a factor before a session is issued.

Both read `hasVerifiedSsoIdentity` and `hasVerifiedSignInPasskey`, each of which was
`Boolean(record?.isVerified)` over the interaction's verification records, with no reference to the
account being signed in. The social identity record carried the same presence-only reading, where
the mandatory profile requirement reads it.

`EnterpriseSsoVerification.isVerified`
(`classes/verifications/enterprise-sso-verification.ts`) is `Boolean(enterpriseSsoUserInfo &&
issuer)`. That class carries no user at all, so such a record counts as verified on the strength of
the assertion alone - whoever it belongs to, and whether or not it resolves to any Logto account.
A `SignInPasskey` record does name the credential's owner, but the policy never compared it.

The verification records are retained across a change of interaction event, by design: a
registration that follows a failed sign-in creates the account from the record the sign-in already
verified. A first-factor record is never re-bound afterwards. Presence was therefore not a safe
proxy for the account under any ordering, and a record left behind by an earlier identification in
the same interaction could reach the policy as well.

For contrast, the second-factor records already carried this rule:
`MfaValidator.getVerifiedMfaVerificationRecords` requires an affirmative owner, and the WebAuthn
MFA route asserts `identifiedUserId === webAuthnVerification.userId`. Enterprise SSO and sign-in
passkey are first-factor records and reach neither.

Reproduced at runtime against the experience API, as integration tests in Logto's own harness: an
account under a mandatory TOTP policy is challenged for its second factor on a password sign-in,
and is not challenged when such a record is present.

## Impact

An account protected by a mandatory MFA policy can be signed into with only a first factor for it
- the exact compromise MFA is deployed to survive. Any tenant that enforces MFA and has enterprise
SSO or passkey sign-in enabled is affected.

The preconditions are lower than the code might suggest. Besides a first factor for the target
account, the attacker needs one of:

- **Enterprise SSO** - a valid assertion from a provider the tenant has configured. It does not
  have to resolve to a Logto account, because such a record is verified without resolving to a
  user.
- **Sign-in passkey** - a passkey they control, registered on an account in the same tenant.

Applies to the `/api/experience/*` interaction API. The deprecated `/api/interaction/*` surface is
not affected.

## Patches

Fixed in 1.46.0.

A verified enterprise SSO or sign-in passkey record now counts for the MFA policy only when it is
the record this interaction established its...

advisories.title: Apple connector trusts the unsigned user.email form field, allowing account takeover
advisories.summary:
### Summary

`@logto/connector-apple` takes a user's email from the `user` field of Apple's sign-in callback in preference to the email claim in Apple's signed ID token. Apple delivers `user` as an ordinary form field that the browser relays to Logto (`response_mode=form_post`), and it is not covered by any signature, so the person signing in can replace it with any address. Logto then treats that address as the Apple account's email.

An attacker with any Apple ID can therefore use a victim's email address to get into the victim's existing Logto account, or to register an account under the victim's address before the victim does.

### Impact

Every tenant that enables the Apple social connector is affected. The attacker needs only their own Apple ID and the victim's email address. The victim does not have to do anything.

- **Takeover of an existing account.** When a social sign-in carries an email that already belongs to a Logto user, Logto offers to link the new social identity to that user, and the linking request is not tied to any proof that the person signing in owns the address. With a forged email, the attacker's Apple ID is linked to the victim's account and the attacker is signed in as the victim.
- **Pre-account takeover.** If no user has the address yet, social sign-up creates a new user with the forged address as its primary email, without verifying it. When the real owner later signs in to that tenant with an email verification code, they land in the account the attacker created, which the attacker can still enter with their Apple ID.

### Patches

Fixed in `@logto/connector-apple` 1.6.11 and Logto 1.46.0. The connector now uses only the email in Apple's signed ID token, and only when Apple marks it as verified.

### Workarounds

Disable the Apple social connector until you can upgrade.

### Details

`packages/connectors/connector-apple/src/index.ts`, `getUserInfo`:

```ts
email:
  user?.email ??
  (payload.email && payload.email_verified === true ? String(payload.email) : undefined),
```

`payload` holds the verified claims of Apple's ID token. `user` is parsed from the callback form data, so `??` lets the unsigned value win. This was introduced in `@logto/connector-apple` 1.2.0 (Logto 1.14.0) by "support apple sign-in with email" (#5454).

Core uses the email the connector returns without verifying it again:

- `packages/core/src/libraries/social.ts`, `findSocialRelatedUser`, looks up an existing user by that email so the identity can be linked to them.
- `packages/core/src/routes/experience/classes/verifications/social-verification.ts`, `toSyncedProfile`, sets it as a new user's `primaryEmail` when no other user has it. The deprecated `/api/interaction` API does the same in `packages/core/src/routes/interaction/actions/helpers.ts`.

Apple includes the `email` claim in the ID token on every authorization when the email scope was granted, so the form field is never needed for the email. Apple may send `email_verified` as either a boolean or the string `"true"`.

advisories.title: Account takeover via email_verified bypass in social account linking (Azure AD, OAuth2 connectors)
advisories.summary:
> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Action required: upgrading alone does not remove the exposure.**
>
> The fix is a configuration option, not a change of default. Logto 1.46.0 adds a `disableEmailSync` option to the OAuth 2.0 connector (`@logto/connector-oauth` 1.8.0). The Azure AD connector has had the same option since 1.43.0. Both default to `false`, so the connector keeps using the email its provider returns until an administrator turns the option on.
>
> If you use the OAuth 2.0 or Azure AD connector with a provider that does not verify email addresses, or lets a user or directory administrator set the email freely, upgrade to 1.46.0 and enable `disableEmailSync` on that connector. The Google, GitHub and OIDC connectors are not affected, because they only return an email that the provider marks as verified.

---

## Summary

When a social sign-in finds an existing account by email, Logto links the social identity and signs the user in without checking whether the social provider asserted the email as verified. An attacker who can present a social identity carrying a victim's email (without owning that mailbox) can take over the victim's account.

The matching SSO path already guards this (`email_verified ?? trustUnverifiedEmail`), and the GitHub connector correctly uses only the verified && primary email - so the social path looks like an oversight rather than intended behavior.

Validated end-to-end locally against `svhd/logto:latest` (core 1.40.1).

## Where (core 1.40.1)

- `packages/core/src/libraries/social.ts` → `findSocialRelatedUser` does `findUserByEmail(info.email)` with no `email_verified` check.
- `packages/core/src/routes/experience/classes/helpers.ts` (case `VerificationType.Social`): when `linkSocialIdentity` is true it uses `identifyRelatedUser()` (the email-matched user).
- `packages/core/src/routes/experience/classes/experience-interaction.ts` `identifyUser()` only calls `guardIdentificationMethod` (method-enablement) - no email-verification gate and no proof of ownership of the matched account.
- `linkSocialIdentity` is a client-supplied request body field (`routes/experience/index.ts`, `POST /api/experience/identification`).

Connectors that let an attacker carry an unverified/attacker-set email:

- `connector-azuread` → `email: conditional(mail)` (Microsoft Graph `mail` is mutable/unverified - the classic nOAuth pattern).
- The standard `connector-oauth2` → surfaces whatever the configured userInfo endpoint maps to `email` via `profileMap`, with no verification check. (This is the connector I used in the PoC.)

(Contrast, safe by default) `connector-github` (verified && primary), `connector-google` and `connector-oidc` only emit the email when the provider marked it verified - so they are not affected unless an admin explicitly opts into `trustUnverifiedEmail` (OIDC). This is exactly why the social-linking path should be checking verification too.

## Validated PoC

(all on localhost, docker compose from the repo)

1. Created a victim user `victim@example.com` (Management API).
2. Configured a standard OAuth2 social connector pointing at a tiny mock IdP I control, whose `/userinfo` returns `{ sub: "attacker-sub-001", email: "victim@example.com" }` - no `email_verified` field (models nOAuth / an unverified-email IdP).
3. Drove the sign-in experience as the "attacker": social verification (Logto fetched my `/userinfo`), then `POST /api/experience/identification` with `{ verificationId, linkSocialIdentity: true }` → 204, then `POST /api/experience/submit` → 200 with a completed sign-in.
4. The victim account's `identities` now contains the attacker's social identity:

   ```json
   "pocoauth2": {
     "userId": "attacker-sub-001",
     "details": { "email": "victim@example.com", ... }
   }
   ```

   The attacker is now signed in as - and permanently linked to - the victim's account.

(Happy to share the mock-IdP + driver script; it's ~3 small files.)

advisories.title: Logto: Account API can disclose stored third-party provider tokens without the identities scope
advisories.summary: Logto is the modern, open-source auth infrastructure for SaaS and AI apps. From 1.31.0 until 1.42.0, the Account API handlers in packages/core/src/routes/account/third-party-tokens.ts allow a caller holding a same-user access token with only the openid scope to retrieve stored social or enterprise SSO provider access tokens through GET /api/my-account/identities/{target}/access-token or GET /api/my-account/sso-identities/{connectorId}/access-token. The handlers authenticate the user but do not require the identities scope that protects neighboring identity-detail operations, bypassing the intended Account API consent boundary. Exploitation requires federated token-set storage to be enabled and the affected user to have authenticated through a supported connector. A low-trust application can use the disclosed provider token against upstream APIs within that token's granted scopes. This issue is fixed in version 1.42.0.

advisories.title: Logto: SSRF via Webhooks and Custom OAuth2 Connector UserInfo Endpoint
advisories.summary: Logto is the modern, open-source auth infrastructure for SaaS and AI apps. Prior to 1.43.0, Logto fetches administrator-controlled outbound destinations without validating the address used for the connection. Webhook delivery in packages/core/src/libraries/hook/utils.ts can reach special-use and cloud metadata addresses. Custom OAuth2 connectors can use an attacker-selected userInfoEndpoint and forward the OAuth access token in the Authorization header, while OIDC connectors can fetch an attacker-selected jwksUri. The affected operations require tenant administrative configuration access, but they cross the server's network boundary and can expose internal data or upstream provider credentials. This issue is fixed in version 1.43.0.

advisories.title: JWT Customizer node:vm execution has no effective timeout, allowing full-process or tenant-wide DoS
Third-party application with only the openid scope can set an initial password on a passwordless, email-less, phone-less account, enabling account takeover
advisories.summary:
### Summary

A third-party OIDC application holding an access token with **only the `openid` scope** could set an initial password on a Logto user account that had no password, no primary email, and no primary phone - without a `logto-verification-id` header or any other security verification.

`POST /api/my-account/password` deliberately skips the verification-record requirement when the account has no existing credential to verify against, so that a social-only or SSO-only user can establish a first password. The exception was correct for its intended caller, the first-party Account Center. But nothing on the route distinguished a first-party caller from a third-party one:

- `koaOidcAuth` gates the whole user router on the `openid` scope alone, and `openid` is unconditionally part of every third-party client's scopes.
- This route has no claim-scope check at all - it is the one Account API route where the scope column is empty. Not even `profile` or `email` is required.

The result is that a plain `openid` authorization, the minimum any OIDC client asks for and the one users are least likely to scrutinize on the consent screen, carried a latent credential-enrollment capability. Once the password exists the exception closes and further changes require verification, so the window is one-shot - but one shot is enough, because the attacker chooses the password and can then sign in directly as the user through the normal username/password flow.

### Preconditions

**This is not exploitable against a default installation, and it is not a consent bypass or an unauthenticated issue.** All of the following must hold:

1. **Account Center is enabled for the tenant.** It ships disabled - `account_centers.enabled` is seeded `false` for every non-admin tenant. While it is off, every Account API route returns `400 account_center.not_enabled` regardless of the caller.
2. **The `password` field is set to `Edit`** in the Account Center field controls. Field controls are seeded empty, so this defaults to off and an admin has to switch it on.
3. **The tenant admin registered the attacker's application as a third-party application** in the tenant.
4. **The end user completed the consent screen** for that application.
5. **The victim account has no password, no primary email, and no primary phone** - the eligibility condition for the initial-password exception. In practice this means a pure social or enterprise-SSO user who has never set a password or verified a contact identifier. Every other account is protected: the same request against an account with any one of those returns `401 verification_record.permission_denied`.

Condition 5 is the real limiter. The affected population is a specific and usually small subset of a tenant's users, and it shrinks over time as users add identifiers.

### Impact

Full account takeover of an eligible user, by an application the user authorized for `openid` only.

The attacker plants a known password on the victim's account, then authenticates as that user through the ordinary username/password sign-in flow - outside the third-party application, with none of the scope restrictions that applied to the original token, and persisting after the user revokes the application's consent.

Reproduced end to end by the reporter on a local deployment of `@logto/core` 1.42.0: `POST /api/my-account/password` with only the third-party Bearer token, no cookies and no verification-record header, returned `204`; the password was persisted and accepted in a fresh username/password login; the same request repeated afterwards returned `401 verification_record.permission_denied`, confirming the exception had closed. No database modification was used to create the vulnerable precondition - the eligible user was produced through a normal social sign-up flow.

### Related surface fixed in the same patch

While fixing the reported route, we audited the rest of the Account API and Verification API...

advisories.title: Token exchange accepts an ID token as an access-token subject and ignores the subject token's issuing client, widening a consented credential into the user's full first-party API authorization
advisories.summary:
### Summary

The OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange grant (`POST /oidc/token`) did not validate what kind of credential it was handed as `subject_token`, nor which client that credential belonged to. Two independent flaws in `validateSubjectToken` let a narrowly consented, client-scoped credential be converted into a broader API access token for the same user.

**1. Token type confusion - an ID token accepted as an access-token subject.** When the subject token is declared as `urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token`, the implementation first tries an opaque-token lookup and, on failure, falls back to JWT verification. That fallback verified only the signature and the `issuer`, then trusted `payload.sub`. OIDC ID tokens are signed by the same keys under the same issuer, so an ID token - an authentication assertion scoped to its relying party, carrying no API authorization - passed the check and resolved to the user. RFC 8693 §2.1/§3 require validation appropriate to the declared type; RFC 8725 §3.12 requires different JWT kinds from one issuer to be mutually exclusive.

**2. Missing first-party check on the subject token's issuing client.** The subject token's issuing client (`token.clientId` on the opaque path, `payload.client_id` on the JWT path) was discarded entirely, so any access token belonging to user U was interchangeable regardless of which client held it. This is exploitable on its own, without any type confusion: a third-party application's ordinary opaque access token could be submitted directly as the subject.

The second flaw is the more consequential of the two, because of what token exchange does with the result. The issued token does **not** inherit the subject token's audience or scopes - it carries the *receiver's* authorization for that user. Third-party applications cannot enable token exchange, so the receiver is always first-party, which means the issued token carries every scope the user's roles grant on the requested resource. A credential the user consented to for one narrow purpose was therefore convertible into the user's full first-party authorization.

The consent boundary is erased; the user's role assignments still bound the result. Scopes the user's roles do not grant are not issued, and the Logto Management API is not reachable this way.

### Preconditions

**This is not exploitable against a default installation, and it is not token forgery or a consent bypass.** All of the following must hold:

1. **A first-party application in the tenant has token exchange enabled.** `allowTokenExchange` defaults to `false` on every new application and an admin must switch it on. With it off, the same request is rejected with `requested grant type is not allowed for this client`.
2. **The attacker controls a client registered in the tenant** whose credentials the victim can be induced to authorize - in the reported scenario, a third-party application onboarded by the tenant admin.
3. **The victim completed authentication or consent** for the attacker's application, yielding a genuine, unexpired, same-issuer token for that user. `openid` alone is sufficient.
4. **The receiver's `client_id` is known.** No client secret is needed: a first-party *public* client (Native or SPA) may enable token exchange, so knowing the public identifier is enough to act as the receiver.
5. **The exchanged scopes are meaningful at a target resource** - the impact is realized only against an API that trusts the tenant's tokens and enforces those scopes.

Signature verification was never bypassed. A tampered token is rejected, and declaring the ID token truthfully as `subject_token_type=...:id_token` is rejected.

### Impact

An attacker-controlled application that the victim authorized for authentication only could obtain an API access token carrying the victim's full first-party authorization on a requested resource, then use it for protected reads and state-changing writes as that user.

advisories.title: Logto Server-Side Request Forgery via OIDC SSO Connector Issuer URL
advisories.summary: Logto through 1.42.0 contains a server-side request forgery vulnerability in the OIDC SSO connector creation endpoint that fails to validate the issuer URL parameter. Tenant administrators with Management API credentials can supply arbitrary internal URLs to trigger HTTP GET requests to private network services, with response content returned in API responses.

advisories.title: Logto Server-Side Request Forgery via webhook test endpoint
advisories.summary: Logto through 1.42.0 contains a server-side request forgery vulnerability in the POST /api/hooks/:id/test endpoint that accepts arbitrary URLs without host validation. Tenant administrators with Management API tokens can make the server issue HTTP POST requests to internal URLs and retrieve response bodies from services on the private network.

advisories.title: Logto: OS command injection vulnerability exists in the Commitlint workflow
advisories.summary: Logto is the modern, open-source auth infrastructure for SaaS and AI apps. From 1.40.1 until 1.41.0, Logto's .github/workflows/commitlint.yml directly interpolated github.event.pull_request.title into the Commitlint on PR title step's inline echo command before piping the title to npx commitlint. A pull request title containing a single quote could terminate the echo string and append arbitrary shell commands on the GitHub Actions runner. The pull_request trigger used a read-only GITHUB_TOKEN and did not expose repository secrets, but injected commands could alter or disrupt the ephemeral workflow execution. This issue is fixed in version 1.41.0.

advisories.title: Unverified email-based SSO account linking
advisories.summary: Logto allows unverified email-based SSO account linking, enabling an attacker to register an identity at a permissive IdP using a victim’s email and gain unauthorized access to the victim’s account.

advisories.title: LOIDC nonce validation bypass
advisories.summary: Logto bypasses OIDC nonce validation when the nonce claim is absent from the id_token, enabling replay of authentication tokens and weakening session-binding.

advisories.title: IdP-initiated SAML sessions not reliably invalidated (replay)
advisories.summary: Logto silently fails to delete IdP-initiated SAML sessions, enabling session replay and reuse within the session’s validity window.

advisories.title: SAML <Conditions> element not validated
advisories.summary: Logto omits validation of the SAML <Conditions> element, enabling attackers to strip time and audience restrictions and replay assertions indefinitely.

advisories.title: Local MFA not enforced during SSO sign-in
advisories.summary: Logto does not enforce locally configured MFA during SSO authentication, allowing users to bypass second-factor requirements and grants unauthorized access.

advisories.title: Principal/domain lookup without case normalization
advisories.summary: Logto performs principal lookup without normalizing email and identifier strings, enabling principal collision and unauthorized account access via case- or Unicode-different identities.

advisories.title: logto-tunnel serves files outside --experience-path via path traversal
advisories.summary: Logto is the modern, open-source auth infrastructure for SaaS and AI apps. Prior to 0.3.9, the Logto Tunnel npm package enabled createStaticFileProxy from packages/tunnel/src/commands/tunnel/index.ts and passed request.url from static asset requests through packages/tunnel/src/commands/tunnel/utils.ts using path.join(staticPath, request.url) and then fs.open(requestPath, "r") without URL normalization or a containment check. When --experience-path was enabled and the tunnel port was reachable, an unauthenticated requester could send a path containing ../ to createStaticFileProxy and read files outside the configured static directory that were readable by the logto-tunnel process. The service used server.listen(port), which could expose the tunnel to other hosts depending on the platform and deployment. This issue is fixed in version 0.3.9.

advisories.title: Logto: Account Center MFA management step-up bypass via WebAuthn registration verification
advisories.summary: Logto is the modern, open-source auth infrastructure for SaaS and AI apps. Prior to 1.41.0, Logto's Account Center step-up check accepted any active verification record that belonged to the current user and had isVerified === true. A WebAuthn registration verification record for binding a new passkey could be created and verified with only an existing Account API bearer token, then sent in the logto-verification-id header and treated as identityVerified=true by Account Center routes, allowing MFA factor management without proving possession of an existing password, identifier, or MFA factor. This issue is fixed in version 1.41.0.

advisories.title: Logto: TOTP code can be replayed within the RFC 6238 validity window (one-time use violation)
advisories.summary: Logto is the modern, open-source auth infrastructure for SaaS and AI apps. Prior to 1.41.0, Logto's existing TOTP verification accepted a successfully used TOTP code again while the code remained inside the RFC 6238 acceptance window because the verifier used otplib's stateless check with window = 1 and did not persist or compare the accepted TOTP time-step counter. An attacker who has the victim's first factor and captures a live TOTP value can replay that value to satisfy MFA during the same acceptance window. This issue is fixed in version 1.41.0.

advisories.title: Logto: ReDoS via unescaped user input in email subaddressing regex (blockSubaddressing)
advisories.summary: Logto is the modern, open-source auth infrastructure for SaaS and AI apps. Prior to 1.41.0, Logto's email subaddressing blocklist in packages/core/src/libraries/sign-in-experience/email-blocklist-policy.ts used the attacker-controlled domain from email input to construct subaddressingRegex when blockSubaddressing was enabled. The permissive emailRegEx accepted multiple at signs and regular expression metacharacters, and POST /api/experience/verification/verification-code could therefore cause catastrophic backtracking in subaddressingRegex.test(email). The resulting event-loop stall could make authentication, token issuance, SSO, and the administrative console unavailable. This issue is fixed in version 1.41.0.

advisories.title: Logto: SAML IdP injects user-controlled profile attributes raw into signed assertions, allowing privilege escalation at relying Service Providers
advisories.summary: Logto is the modern, open-source auth infrastructure for SaaS and AI apps. Prior to 1.41.0, Logto's self-hosted SAML application IdP built the signed SAML response and assertion by string-substituting user-controlled profile attributes such as name, email, and custom attribute-mapping values into element-text placeholders of a SAML XML template using samlify 2.10.0, which left those placeholders unescaped. An authenticated low-privilege user could place XML markup in a profile attribute so Logto signed a forged SAML attribute, such as an arbitrary role, allowing privilege escalation at relying Service Providers that authorize on SAML attributes. This issue is fixed in version 1.41.0.

advisories.title: Logto: XSS via unescaped RelayState in SAML auto-submit form
advisories.summary: Logto is the modern, open-source auth infrastructure for SaaS and AI apps. Prior to 1.41.0, @logto/core reflected the SAML RelayState, SAMLResponse, and actionUrl into a Logto-origin auto-submit HTML form in packages/core/src/saml-application/SamlApplication/utils.ts without HTML-attribute escaping. A SAML application flow with a crafted RelayState from GET or POST /api/saml/:id/authn could inject script that runs on the Logto tenant origin after the user completes login. This issue is fixed in version 1.41.0.
